readings.c1s3:
¶
'''tremulousness''' (trem′ụ̄-lus-nes), ''n.'' The state of being tremulous.

{{smaller block|''Tremulousness'' of voice is very effectively used by some vocalists in highly pathetic passages.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Universal Progress, p. 222.}}}}

'''tren<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''trennen'', < MD. ''trennen'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''trennen'', separate, factitive of OHG. *''trinnan'', MHG. ''trinnen'', separate.] To separate.

{{smaller block|Uch toth fram other is ''trent.''
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', II. 212.}}}}

'''tren<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' [Origin not ascertained.] A fish-spear. ''Ainsworth.''

'''trenail''', ''n.'' A form of ''treenail.''

'''trench''' (trench), ''v.'' [< ME. *''trenchen'', *''tranchen'', ''traunchen'', < OF. ''trencher'', ''trancher'', F. ''trancher'' = Pr. ''trencar'', ''trenchar'', ''trinquar'' = Sp. ''trinchar'', chop, ''trincar'', carve, = Pg. ''trinchar'', carve, ''trincar'', crack, break, = It. ''trinciare'', cut, carve, hew, slice, OIt. ''trinceare'', trench, ''trincare'', trim; prob. < L. ''truncare'' (LL. *''trincare'', ML. (after Rom.) ''trencare''), cut off, lop: see ''truncate'', ''trunk'', ''v.'' Hence ''trench'', ''n.'', ''trenchant'', ''intrench'', ''retrench'', etc.] I. ''trans.'' 1†. To cut, as a notch, hole, mark, etc.; form by cutting; carve; incise.

{{smaller block|''Traunche'' that sturgyon.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 265.}}}}

{{smaller block|This weak impress of love is as a figure
''Trenched'' in ice.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 2. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|View the wound, by cruel knife
''Trench'd'' into him.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 2.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
2. To cut into; form a ditch, trench, or other linear depression in: as, to ''trench'' the ground round a camp or a fort.

{{smaller block|Pioneers, with spade and pickaxe arm'd,
Forerun the royal camp, to ''trench'' a field,
Or cast a rampart.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 677.}}}}

{{smaller block|And ''trench'' the strong, hard mould with the spade,
Where never before a grave was made.
{{right|''Bryant'', Two Graves.}}}}

{{smaller block|We found that the older trachytic lavas of the hills had been deeply ''trenched'' by lateral valleys.
{{right|''A. Geikie'', Geol. Sketches, x.}}}}

3. In ''agri.'', to furrow deeply, especially with the spade; dig deeply and turn over thoroughly by means of a succession of contiguous trenches.

{{smaller block|In order to expedite the growth of ivy, the ground, previously to planting, should be ''trenched'' two feet deep.
{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LVIII. 264.}}}}

4. In ''cabinet-making'' and the like, to work with a long continuous groove, as a rail which is to be fitted upon the heads of a series of bars or balusters.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To cut; slash.

{{smaller block|Temir the stout
Rider who with sharpe
''Trenching'' blade of bright steele
Hath made his fiercest foes to feele . . .
The strength of his braue right arme.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie (ed. Arber), p. 107.}}}}

2. Specifically, to form a trench or trenches; proceed by or as if by means of trenches.

{{smaller block|An underground passage constructed by ''trenching'' down from the surface.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 622.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
2†. A lane or road cut through shrubbery or woods.

{{smaller block|And in a ''trench'' forth in the park goth she.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire's Tale, l. 384.}}}}

'''Returns of a trench.''' See ''return''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Tail of the trenches.''' See ''tail''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To mount the trenches,''' to mount guard in the trenches: usually done at night.—'''To open the trenches,''' to begin to form the lines of approach to a fortified place.—'''To scour the trenches,''' to make a sally upon the guard, force them to give way, drive off the working party, break down the parapet, fill up the trenches, and spike the cannon. ''Wilhelm'', Mil. Encyc.

'''trenchancy''' (tren′chan-si), ''n.'' [< ''trenchan(t)'' + ''-cy.''] The state or quality of being trenchant; sharpness; keenness; causticity.

{{smaller block|Mrs. Elsmere was old enough to know what importance to attach to the ''trenchancy'' of eighteen.
{{right|''Mrs. Humphry Ward'', Robert Elsmere, iv.}}}}

'''trenchant''' (tren′chant), ''a.'' [< ME. ''trenchant'', ''trenchaunt'', < OF. ''trenchant'', F. ''tranchant'', ppr. of ''trencher'', cut: see ''trench'', ''v.''] 1. Cutting; sharp; keen.

{{smaller block|By his belt he baar a long panade,
And of a swerd ful ''trenchant'' was the blade.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve's Tale, l. 10}}
Let not the virgin's cheek
Make soft thy ''trenchant'' sword.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 115.}}}}

2. Penetrating; energetic; downright.

{{smaller block|I too have longed for ''trenchant'' force,
And will like a dividing spear.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Switzerland, iv., A Farewell.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
{{smaller block|Sworn foe of Cant, he smote it down
With ''trenchant'' wit unsparing.
{{right|''Whittier'', Randolph of Roanoke.}}}}

{{smaller block|The . . . sun was warm, and the air was bland, with only now and then a ''trenchant'' breath from the Alps.
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xviii.}}}}

{{smaller block|That ''trenchant'' policy of "reconstruction" which followed close upon the termination of the war.
{{right|''W. Wilson'', Cong. Gov., i.}}}}

3. Specifically, in ''zoöl.'', sectorial, as a molar or premolar; sharp-edged: as, the ''trenchant'' canines of a saber-toothed tiger.

'''trenchantly''' (tren′chant-li), ''adv.'' In a trenchant manner; cuttingly; sharply; keenly.

'''trench-cart''' (trench′kärt), ''n.'' ''Milit.'', a cart adapted to pass along the trenches, to distribute ammunition and other supplies. It is mounted on low wheels so as not to be exposed to the enemy's fire.

'''trench-cavalier''' (trench′kav-a-lēr″), ''n.'' ''Milit.'', a high parapet of gabions, fascines, earth, etc., erected by besiegers upon the glacis to command and enfilade the covered way of a fortress.

'''trencher<sup>1</sup>''' (tren′chėr), ''n.'' [< ME. *''trenchour'', < OF. *''trencheor'' (ML. reflex ''trencheator''), < ''trencher'', cut: see ''trench'', ''v.'' In def. 2 taken as < ''trench'', ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] 1†. One who carves at table; also, one who carves at a side-table for the company.

{{smaller block|I was not born, I take it, for a ''trencher'',
Nor to espouse my mistress' dairy-maid.
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Noble Gentleman, iii. 1.}}}}

2. One who cuts or digs trenches; a trench-digger or -maker.
readings.c3s3:
¶

3. That which trenchers contain; food; hence, the pleasures of the table: often used attributively.

{{smaller block|Those ''trencher'' philosophers which in the later age of the Roman state were usually in the houses of great persons.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''trencher'' fury of a riming parasite.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, Pref., ii.}}}}

4. Same as ''trencher-cap''.—'''Trencher salt-cellar.''' {{smaller|See ''salt-cellar''.}}

'''trencher-bread†''' (tren′chėr-bred), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trenchor brede''; < ''trencher''<sup>2</sup> + ''bread''<sup>1</sup>.] A kind of coarse bread, slices of which were used as plates for other food at table. See ''trencher''<sup>2</sup>, 2.

{{smaller block|Item, that the ''Trenchor Brede'' be maid of the Meale as it cummyth frome the Milne.
{{right|Quoted in ''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 125, Index.}}}}

'''trencher-buffoon†''' (tren′chėr-bu-fön″), ''n.'' One who amuses persons at their meals; the wag of a company.

'''trencher-cap''' (tren′chėr-kap), ''n.'' A cap of the peculiar form worn by professors and students at some universities; a mortar-board.

'''trencher-chaplain†''' (tren′chėr-chap″lạ̄n), ''n.'' A domestic chaplain. ''Heylin.''

'''trencher-coat''' (tren′chėr-kōt), ''n.'' In ''gilding'', a preparatory coating applied before the gold-leaf is laid on. It consists of Armenian bole, bloodstone, and galena, mixed up in water, with a little olive-oil.

And healthy life alone did paint her cheek.
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 115.}}}}

{{smaller block|Contortions of the face, and an irregular movement of the body and extremities, with ''tremors'' of greater or less violence.{{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 128.}}}}

3. A trembling, quivering, or quavering quality or effect: as, a ''tremor'' of light.

{{smaller block|To detect, as one or another addressed me, the ''tremor'' of a voice which, in long-past days, had been wont to bellow through a speaking-trumpet.{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 14.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Intention tremor,''' a tremor developed in a part when it moves to do something.—'''Mercurial tremor,''' a tremulous condition of the system caused by exposure to mercurial vapors; mercurial palsy; the trembles.—'''Neural tremors.''' See ''neural.''—'''Purring tremor.''' Same as ''purring thrill'' (which see, under ''purr''<sup>1</sup>). ='''Syn. 2.''' ''Trepidation, Emotion,'' etc. (see ''agitation''), quiver, quivering, quaking. See ''trepidation.''}}

'''tremorless''' (trem′ọr-les), ''a.'' [< ''tremor'' + ''-less.''] Free from tremor or vibration.

{{smaller block|The plain of the Channel sea stretched flat on either hand of me, ''tremorless'' as ebony.{{right|''The Portfolio'', N. S., No. 1, p. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|The . . . ''tremorless'' atmosphere of eternal silence.{{right|''G. Kennan'', The Century, XXXV. 756.}}}}

'''tremulant''' (trem′ū-lant), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= It. ''tremolante'', < ML. ''tremulan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''tremulare'', tremble: see ''tremble.'' Cf. ''tremulous.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Trembling.

{{smaller block|Hapless De Brézé; doomed to survive long ages, in men's memory, in this faint way, with ''tremulent'' [read ''tremulant''] white rod!{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., I. v. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''music'', same as ''tremolo'' (''d'').

'''tremulation''' (trem-ū-lā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ML. *''tremulatio(n-)'', < ''tremulare'', tremble: see ''tremulant.''] A trembling; a tremulous condition. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|I was struck with such a terrible ''tremulation'' that it was as much as three gulps of my brandy bottle could do to put my chill'd blood into its regular motion.
{{right|''Tom Brown'', Works, II. 236. (''Davies.'')}}}}

¶
'''tremulous''' (trem′ū-lus), ''a.'' [= Sp. ''trémulo'' = Pg. ''tremulo'' = It. ''tremulo, tremolo'', < L. ''tremulus'', shaking, quivering, < ''tremere'', shake, tremble: see ''tremble''.] 1. Trembling; shaking; quivering; vibrating; unsteady.

{{smaller block|A sober calm
Fleeces unbounded ether, whose least wave
Stands ''tremulous''. {{right|''Thomson'', Autumn, l. 958.}}}}

{{smaller block|Think of honeyed words and ''tremulous'' touch
As things that slay.
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 333.}}}}

{{smaller block|Every fibre is alive with feeling and ''tremulous'' with radiant thought. {{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 114.}}}}

{{smaller block|That old ''tremulous'' laugh which was half a cough.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xx.}}}}

2. Lacking firmness, resolution, or courage; feeble; wavering; timid.

{{smaller block|The tender ''tremulous'' Christian is easily distracted and amazed by them. {{right|''Decay of Christian Piety.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Those dry, forlorn, ''tremulous'' specimens of female mortality which abound in every village congregation.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 56.}}}}

3. In ''entom.'', finely wavy: as, a ''tremulous'' line.—'''Tremulous poplar.''' {{smaller|Same as ''trembling poplar''. See ''poplar''.}}

'''tremulously''' (trem′ū-lus-li), ''adv.'' In a tremulous manner.

{{smaller block|So linger, as from me earth's light withdraws,
Dear touch of Nature, ''tremulously'' bright!
{{right|''Lowell'', The Eye's Treasury.}}}}

'''tremulousness''' (trem′ụ̄-lus-nes), ''n.'' The state of being tremulous.

{{smaller block|''Tremulousness'' of voice is very effectively used by some vocalists in highly pathetic passages.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Universal Progress, p. 222.}}}}

'''trenail''', ''n.'' A form of ''treenail.''

'''3.''' To encroach; infringe; obtrude as if by cutting into something: used of conduct, expression, or the like, usually with ''on'' or ''upon'': as, to ''trench upon'' another's rights. Also ''intrench.''

{{smaller block|The boy with buttons, and the basket-wench,
To vent their wares into my works do ''trench!''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Time Vindicated.}}
Madam, I am bold
To ''trench'' so far ''upon'' your privacy.
{{right|''Massinger'', Bashful Lover, i. 1.}}}}

'''4†.''' To reach out; extend; tend.

{{smaller block|Many times the things deduced to judgment may be "meum" and "tuum," when the reason and consequence thereof may ''trench'' to point of estate.
{{right|''Bacon'', Judicature (ed. 1887).}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' 3. ''Encroach upon, Infringe'', etc. See ''trespass.''}}

'''trench''' (trench), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trench, trenche'', < OF. *''trenche'', a trench (cf. OF. ''trenche, tranche'', a slice, also a pruning-knife) (OF. also ''trenchee'', F. ''tranchée'' = It. ''trincea'', a trench), < ''trencher'', cut: see ''trench'', ''n.''] '''1.''' A narrow excavation of considerable length cut into the earth; a deep furrow or ditch. {{smaller|In agriculture trenches are made for drainage, for loosening the soil deeply, for certain kinds of planting, etc. In military operations trenches constitute the parallels or approaches used for the shelter of besieging troops, as before a fortified place, or for protection and defense, as in an intrenched camp. If the ground is hard or rocky, trenches are raised above it with fascines, bags of earth, etc.; but if the earth can be easily dug, then a ditch or way is sunk, and edged with a parapet, next to the enemy, formed by the earth thrown out of the ditch. The depth of the trench, form of the parapet, etc., vary according to the purpose or occasion.}}

{{smaller block|There is a very strong and great Castle, invironed with exceeding deepe ''trenches'' and a strong wall.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 9.}}}}

2†. A lane or road cut through shrubbery or woods.

{{smaller block|And in a ''trench'' forth in the park goth she.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire's Tale, l. 384.}}}}

{{smaller block|All these works were executed by the soldiers, who showed themselves excellent ''trenchers.''

'''trencher<sup>2</sup>''' (tren′chėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trenchere'', ''trenchor'', ''trenchour'', < OF. ''trenchoir'', ''trencheoir'', a trencher, lit. a cutting-place, < ''trencher'', cut: see ''trench'', ''v.''] 1. A wooden plate or platter (originally a square piece of board or slice of wood) for the table or the kitchen. {{smaller|Trenchers of some form were used at table till a late period, at first by all classes and afterward by the common people, either to be eaten from or for the cutting up of food; and the number of changes of them during a meal in early times was regulated by personal rank. Trenchers and plates are sometimes mentioned together in later writings, the food being probably served from the former to the latter.}}

{{smaller block|Thus ye shall serue your soueraync: laye [six or eight] ''trenchours'', & yf he be of a lower degre [or] estate, laye fyue ''trenchours'', & yf he be of lower degre, foure ''trenchours'', & of an other degre, thre ''trenchovrs.''
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 274.}}
We had no napkins nor change of ''trenchers'', and drunk out of earthen pitchers and wooden dishes.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Oct. 29, 1663.}}
To heap the ''trencher'' and to fill the caup of an idle blackguard ne'er-do-weel.
{{right|''Scott'', Pirate, iv.}}}}

2†. A slice of bread used as a platter to lay food upon, as thin cakes of bread still are in some countries. {{smaller|Such slices of bread were either eaten after the meat placed upon them, or, as commonly among the rich, thrown into an alms-basket, with other leavings, for the poor.}}

{{smaller block|Loaves at this period [the 14th century] were made of a secondary quality of flour, and these were first pared, and then cut into thick slices, which were called in French tranchoirs, and in English ''trenchers'', because they were to be carved upon.
{{right|''Wright'', Homes of Other Days, xi.}}}}

'''trencher-buffoon†''' (tren′chėr-bu-fön″), ''n.'' One who amuses persons at their meals; the wag of a company.

'''trencher-cap''' (tren′chėr-kap), ''n.'' A cap of the peculiar form worn by professors and students at some universities; a mortar-board.

'''trencher-chaplain†''' (tren′chėr-chap″lạ̄n), ''n.'' A domestic chaplain. ''Heylin.''

'''trencher-coat''' (tren′chėr-kōt), ''n.'' In ''gilding'', a preparatory coating applied before the gold-leaf is laid on. It consists of Armenian bole, bloodstone, and galena, mixed up in water, with a little olive-oil.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
